The post Last call! Cap Classique, Sauvignon Blanc and Rosé entries close at midnight, 11 Nov appeared first on winemag.
content:
Category Reports, sponsored by Prescient Fund Services, are being released across four seasonal series: Autumn, Winter, Spring and Summer. The first three are now complete, with Summer still to come.

The following reports are now open for entry (click the report name for details):

Cap Classique

Sauvignon Blanc and Sauv-Sem blends

Rosé

The wines will be tasted by editor Christian Eedes, Ndaba Dube, Director of Operations, President Hotel, Cape Town, Spencer Foundaumiere, wine entrepreneur and ASI Diploma Sommelier, and wine writer Malu Lambert.

Why enter?

  • Your wine is judged blind, without producer or brand influencing the result.
  • Every entry receives a Winemag 100-point score.
  • The Top 10 receive individual tasting notes.
  • Inclusion in a buyer’s guide, ranking wines by quality relative to price.
  • Your wine is assessed alongside other leading examples in its category.
  • Best Overall recognition goes to the highest-performing wine in the tasting.

Entry fee: R1,495 per wine, including VAT.

Prize

The producer of the best wine overall in each of the respective categories wins shipping services worth R10 000 from Aspiring Couriers.

title: Editorial: How long can South African white wines age?
summary:
“The hype is real,” was my observation on X after recently opening a bottle of Palladius 2021, the white blend from Sadie Family Wines. The wine had shed the precociousness of youth without yet acquiring any significant developed character. “Five years from vintage is good for me, rather than too little, too late,” I concluded. […]

The post Editorial: How long can South African white wines age? appeared first on winemag.
content:
“The hype is real,” was my observation on X after recently opening a bottle of Palladius 2021, the white blend from Sadie Family Wines. The wine had shed the precociousness of youth without yet acquiring any significant developed character. “Five years from vintage is good for me, rather than too little, too late,” I concluded.

Would the winemaker agree? The comprehensive tasting note for the 2021 vintage available online advises: “As always, it is suggested to age this wine for a minimum of 4–6 years.”

There are few things more difficult in wine criticism than proposing a drinking window. Readers quite reasonably want to know when a wine is likely to be at its best, but the honest answer is that nobody knows with any great certainty. We can make educated guesses, draw on experience and point to certain indicators, but predicting the future of a wine is an inexact science at best.

Ian Naudé, a stalwart of the Cape’s boutique scene, opened a tasting of his current releases this past Friday with something unexpected: the 2009 vintage of his white blend (55% Chenin Blanc, 25% Sauvignon Blanc, 20% Semillon). I was amazed to find that has not only survived but is prospering, nearly two decades on from vintage. Still available at R500 a bottle.

Just how relative ageing potential can be was demonstrated later that same day, when a bottle of Huet Le Haut-Lieu Demi-Sec 1962 was opened over lunch. Still very much intact, it showed notes of bergamot, apricot and honey. Sixty-four years had only added to the drinking experience.

When is a wine at its best?

My own preference, especially when it comes to modern-era South African white wine, is to err on the side of caution. Rather drink a wine wondering what it might yet still become than regretting what it must have been like in its prime. Put another way, rather a year too early than a day too late. There is something particularly dispiriting about opening a bottle that has passed its best. The promise is gone, and all that remains is a rather forlorn reminder of what might have been.

Of course, this assumes that we can agree on what constitutes a wine being at its best in the first place. The appreciation of developed white wine, with its tertiary characteristics of deep colour, bee’s wax, nuts, mushroom, earth and all manner of other savoury nuances, is even more subjective than usual. Some drinkers find these qualities fascinating, others regard them as evidence of decline. There is no objective point at which a wine moves from being mature to being over the hill, and the transition is not necessarily a particularly orderly one.

A good old wine, however, is one of the great pleasures of being interested in wine. More than that, it is a reminder of what is at stake when we judge young wine. It is not simply a question of what is in the glass today, but what that wine might become. Often the distance between the two is considerable.

This is one reason why assessing the ageing potential of a wine is such a precarious business. We are effectively being asked to predict how a complex biological product will evolve over a period of years, sometimes decades, based on a relatively brief encounter at a particular moment in its development. Even with a detailed knowledge of the producer, vineyard, vintage and winemaking, there are simply too many variables.

Certain broad generalisations hold true. Wines with good acidity, sufficient phenolics where appropriate, concentration and structural balance tend to have a better chance of ageing gracefully. But these are indicators rather than guarantees. Grand wines can disappoint, while relatively modest wines can prove surprisingly rewarding. Anyone who has spent time opening bottles from a mixed cellar will have encountered both phenomena.

The limits of prediction

I’m no viticulturist, but two things seem to matter most: vine stress and the ripeness window. Severe drought, heat and low soil nitrogen are common in much of the Cape, and badly stressed vines seem more prone to producing wines that fade early. Pick too early and you risk green, unripe wines; pick too late and you get flabby, low-acid wines that oxidise easily. The best ageing whites usually come from fruit with real flavour development and still decent acidity, which is harder to achieve where heat pushes sugar up and acidity down before flavour has caught up.

All of which makes the business of publishing drinking windows something of a fool’s errand. A producer’s track record is perhaps as useful a guide as any when deciding which wines are likely to reward patience, but even this offers no guarantees. Storage conditions matter enormously, and two bottles of the same wine, even from the same case, can develop differently. Cork, in particular, introduces an element of unpredictability with which all of us are familiar.

You may have noticed that I don’t propose drinking windows. There are simply too many variables for the exercise to mean much. The one principle I would urge on readers is this: don’t become so preoccupied with waiting for a wine to reach its supposed peak that you miss the pleasure of drinking it along the way. Opening a bottle a little too soon is a small sin. Opening it a little too late is rather harder to forgive.

title: Michael Fridjhon: SA wine has the infrastructure. Where are the sales?
summary:
The recent editorial entitled “The Stormers get it. The Proteas less so. What can wine learn?” on Winemag.co.za, which proposed a business case for the wine industry based on the recent commercial success of the Stormers, was glib but not wholly misdirected. Even before that editorial appeared, the state of our wine industry had been […]

The post Michael Fridjhon: SA wine has the infrastructure. Where are the sales? appeared first on winemag.
content:
The recent editorial entitled “The Stormers get it. The Proteas less so. What can wine learn?” on Winemag.co.za, which proposed a business case for the wine industry based on the recent commercial success of the Stormers, was glib but not wholly misdirected.

Even before that editorial appeared, the state of our wine industry had been on my mind. However, unlike Christian, I wasn’t nearly as concerned about its performance. For a start, while the decline (7.7% in 2025) in domestic sales definitely reflects the cutback in consumer spending, the home market is not in free fall. The figures look bad in the face of the international average – which is only 2.7% – but it’s also not out of line with many important markets. Wine consumption fell by 9.4% in Italy, 4% in the USA, 4.2% in Germany, 2.5% in Britain and 12.7% in the Netherlands.

Economies with a more substantial middle-class component – so therefore less exposed to the effect of tough times on discretionary spending – held up better. The UK, USA and Germany saw a combined volume decline of under 4%. China lost 13%, Argentina dropped 18% and Spain 8.1%.

Considering South Africa’s Gini co-efficient (the measure of inequality in the economy), the lack of economic growth, the ANC government’s prohibitionist agenda and the political uncertainty which pervades the thinking of those South Africans who do not live in the Western Cape bubble, it’s hard to attribute the numbers to mismanagement and incompetence. Eedes – squinting through his Western Cape lens – suggests that wine is declining in relevance to people who once regarded it as essential to their everyday life. Consumption may be down in the leafy suburbs of the Mother City but it’s holding up quite well in the pot-holed streets of Gauteng.

The domestic wine market is made up of many components and several of them interact in ways which are beyond whoever might be responsible for managing the future of the industry. When times are tough wine drinkers on the breadline gravitate to the cheapest available beverage. Mostly this is product outside the reach of those who gather the statistics. So-called ales (sugar-fermented beverages) are a first substitute, so is illicit bulk wine sold out of the back of the cellar in plastic jugs, with no excise recorded or paid. Given the size of the illicit market, it’s worth testing whether the measured decline in sales is reflected by an exact and commensurate increase in the industry’s stocks on hand. I’ll bet a papsak of your choice that they don’t.

This brings us to the question of who actually runs the wine industry, and why the analogy with the Stormers (or any other company) simply doesn’t work. The South African wine industry is not a business in a way that a rugby franchise or a gold mine is one. Even if it were desirable to configure it as such (and I’m not denying there’s a case to be made for a more coherent structure) as things stand this is simply not possible.

For a start, there’s no commercial connection between the many moving parts. There are the bits that have to be done by some statutory authority, there are the marketing efforts of the producers, and by appointed entities (representative organisations such as WoSA, for example, but also Stellenbosch Wine Routes, CWG etc), and there are actual sales in which only the producer or distributor has a financial interest. In the bad old days you could conceivably argue for an umbrella organisation like KWV to do it all. Only the now-defunct Communist Eastern Bloc ran a single sales channel for a nation’s wine – and we know how that ended.

When things aren’t going well it’s tempting to find someone to blame other than yourself – like SA Wine or WoSA – or the government which doesn’t do enough to support the wine industry, or the retailers who, with unspeakable cruelty, chase the best deal at the expense of the more naive craft producers. It’s true that at the moment there does appear to be a low-key war between the two bodies (SA Wine and the Wine Certification Authority) both of whom might function more effectively if they were less obsessed with territory. But it doesn’t explain the current predicament.

SA Wine is doing a pretty solid job ensuring that growers and producers work as scientifically and cost-effectively as possible. But it’s not there to sell their wine for them. There’s no real support for domestic sales (and until now there’s also been no money for such an entity). That’s what producers the world over have to manage on their own – the same as if you sell magazines or widgets.

On the export front it’s easy to point out WoSA’s failures (and to forget its successes). But it also has an infinitesimally small budget for the size of the task it confronts. The current management has inherited most of the focus markets. And that inheritance was partly influenced by the preferences of the producers who participated in or led the market selections. So since 1994 everyone has been plugging away at the UK, the Netherlands, Germany, Scandinavia, Canada, China and the USA (which were more fun but less cost effective to travel to than Gauteng). Last year we lost much of the USA – no one at SA Wine or WoSA was to blame for that. And we haven’t yet been able to tap into the China duty-free benefit because it seems SARS has been dragging its feet in providing the certifications demanded by the Chinese.

So arguably we’ve been great at building competences and skills and we’ve not been very good at building sales. Industry institutions are expected to create appropriate infrastructure, establish vehicles for training and skills transfer, and maintain product integrity. Hard to fault anything here. WoSA has managed the thankless task of facilitating exports on a ludicrously small budget. I’ve no doubt that a better job could have been done, but not by an institutionalised bureaucracy. Sales (local and international) have been stumbling for some time. A one-line diagnosis here would be that as an industry we “other” the consumer rather than include consumer expectations in our thinking. In addition, very few of the key decision-makers spend any real time in the biggest wine market in the world for Cape wine – which is Gauteng.

So in my view – and to use Christian’s Stormers’ analogy – the corporate machine is doing what it’s supposed to be doing. It’s the players who keep fumbling the ball and missing the chances. The fact that some are doing really well (while others aren’t) tells us that the team is a disparate blend of stars and mediocrities. Not everyone in the class can realistically get a distinction, so perhaps we should also consider failures. Here, compared with other wine industries around the world, we’ve had remarkably few bankruptcies. I guess, in South Africa at least, die agteros kom ook in die kraal.

  • Michael Fridjhon has over thirty-five years’ experience in the liquor industry. He is the founder of Winewizard.co.za and holds various positions including Visiting Professor of Wine Business at the University of Cape Town; founder and director of WineX – the largest consumer wine show in the Southern Hemisphere and chairman of The Trophy Wine Show.

title: Tim James: Three cool Pinotages for a hot summer
summary:
I rather surprised myself last week, when writing about wine-grape crosses, by suggesting that pinotage is, both internationally and locally, an unusually successful one. I think it might be worth repeating as I don’t recall this competitive point being made last year, despite all the rah-rah about the centenary of Perold’s bringing together of cinsaut […]

The post Tim James: Three cool Pinotages for a hot summer appeared first on winemag.
content:
I rather surprised myself last week, when writing about wine-grape crosses, by suggesting that pinotage is, both internationally and locally, an unusually successful one. I think it might be worth repeating as I don’t recall this competitive point being made last year, despite all the rah-rah about the centenary of Perold’s bringing together of cinsaut and pinot noir.

As with so many crossings, his aim was to unite the quality of the one grape with the high yield and vineyard strength of the other. But what was unusual was that in pinotage’s case it worked. I don’t want to exaggerate things, but the past decade or two have shown that Kanonkop’s earlier shining success with the grape while there was so much unsuccess (and sneering) all around was not a totally weird anomaly. We are still stuck with a lot of over-ambitious, over-ripe, over-oaked, big, too-tannic, and heavy wines. They do win some awards but not a whole lot of friends and admirers internationally and among more sophisticated locals. But there are now so many excellent examples of pinotage, so well made, in a range of styles from light hipsterness to long-lived grandeur that we can surely accept that the grape itself need no longer be called “controversial”.

And pinotage has been successful in the wine industry, and its place is surely secure. And that’s not true, as I suggested, of most crossings in the longer term. Certainly not in South Africa, and this suggests that pinotage’s achievement was not due only to the Afrikaner nationalist hype around it (that arguably did more harm than good, especially in the over-ambitious and inappropriate treatment given the wine). In terms of hopes for the cross, pinotage is inevitably not as great a grape as pinot noir, but I would be inclined to argue, based on the evidence, that it is a superior wine-grape to cinsaut: there are, surely, more excellent pinotages around than there are cinsauts (though there certainly are some of the latter) – but that would be fun to have an argument about.

I was vaguely thinking about pinotage as I wandered into the small wine department at my local branch of Woolworths. And I was also vaguely noticing that the selection looked better and more interesting than it did a year or two back, when I remember thinking it had declined. Those two vague thoughts coalesced into something approaching focus when I noticed a big, familiar B on a label amongst the pinotages. I thought at first that it must be Bruwer Vintners Liberté, long one of my favourites. But I put on my glasses (which helps combat some aspects of vagueness) and saw it was indeed Bruwer Vintners, but a wine called Private Reserve Pinotage and at a comparatively modest price (R170).

So then I had to call in at my first-class local wine-shop, Constantia Wine and Craft, where I knew I’d find a bottle of Liberté for purposes of comparison; I did indeed, the 2022 at R446. And also snatched up, to have an outsider present, a bottle of Lemberg Pinotage 2022, appealingly priced at R100. It made for an enjoyable little tasting with my friend Wesley (who makes a pleasant modest pinotage himself, brandishing a Flying Pug on the label – but it seldom gets beyond the ambit of his own very active corkscrew).

All three proved to be in the more modern style of pinotage: fresh, without obvious oaking, stressing fruit charm, tannins far from overweening, the alcohol levels neither too low for vinosity nor too high for liveliness. Lemberg’s declaration of alcohol was the highest at 13.5%, but in fact it’s much closer to the 13% on the other labels. With a little perfume, red-fruited, light-feeling, a properly dry finish and an easy-going tannic grip, it is a delicious wine. No great intensity, but that’s part of its unpretentious good balance. Really excellent value, I think, and I’m pleased my hand lighted on it in the shop. It will do so again – more deliberately next time.

Bruwer Vintners Private Reserve has rather darker fruit, and a greater feeling of depth and fullness of flavour to it, supported by a slightly firmer tannic grip, and also blissfully dry. Altogether unsurprising to a long-time admirer of Liberté. From Stellenbosch vines, while Liberté is fimly rooted in Polkadraai Hills. Gavin Bruwer tells me that Woolworths, having done a wide-ranging tasting of pinotages, approached them to produce something in a more modern, lighter and fruit-driven style, as a tribute to the grape’s centenary. As one of great ambassadors of new-wave pinotage, he relished the opportunity. It’s a lovely wine and generously priced. Gavin says that there’s something of a promotion of the wine due, but even without it this is very good value. And, happily, it’s not a one-off: 2025 has also been made.

The only problem with moving on to Liberté 2022 is that it puts the Reserve in its place. You’re paying well for it (though not outrageously), so it should. A few years have added to its depth, complexity and refinement. There’s a bit more of everything here. More whole-bunch fruit has added to the perfume; there’s no overt concentration – that’s not what this wine is about – but there’s a completeness of fruit in balance with the refined but firm tannic structure and making for a graceful and compelling whole, long-lingering, understated in its seriousness. The wine was even better on the second day, especially the aromatic pleasure it gave – a sign that this wine should develop well for some years (longevity is something associated with pinotage, another aspect of its claims).

As the hot weather starts intruding, it’s worth remembering that all three of these wines can, perhaps should, be drunk fairly cool. Not cold (though Lemberg would be most suited to that), definitely not chilled. But if you’re having a bottle at some restaurant over lunch or on a warm evening, don’t be shy to ask for an ice-bucket to plonk the bottle in occasionally. In fact, generally, be reminded that many restaurants will want to serve their reds too warm, for the sake of their own ease. Don’t let them. And don’t forget your own fridge – sometimes you’ll forget to take the bottle out before it’s too cold, but it’ll warm up again only too quickly.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.
